MARKET.head: Texas High Plains growers struggle as wineries cut grape purchases
MARKET.summ: As Texas wines earn broader recognition, the High Plains growers behind much of that progress are navigating a market correction that could shape the state’s next chapter
takeaways: Texas wineries saw explosive sales from 2020 to early 2023, then demand softened and inventories backed up, leaving High Plains growers with unsold fruit.
Growers including Katy Jane Seaton at Farmhouse Vineyards now tier vineyard care by contract status, reserving premium farming for committed buyers only.
Multi-year contracts have become rare; some wineries wait until harvest to buy cheaper fruit on the spot market, forcing growers to plan without certainty.
Producers like Connor Wilmeth at Lahey Vineyards and Kim McPherson of McPherson Cellars are seeking East Coast buyers to reduce dependence on local Hill Country wineries.
Veteran growers including Jet Wilmeth and Neal Newsom are considering retirement or reduced operations, threatening continuity of benchmark vineyard sites.

MARKET.head: English estates launch prestige sparkling cuvées at Champagne price points
MARKET.summ: Are English prestige cuvées worth prices that rival the top end of Champagne?
takeaways: Nyetimber, Chapel Down, Gusbourne, Langham and Squerryes have released prestige cuvées priced £100 to £395, mimicking Champagne's luxury positioning and production model.
Nyetimber launched England's first prestige cuvée in 2018, the 1086 range, after proprietor Eric Heerema acquired the West Sussex estate in 2006 with this ambition.
Extended lees ageing, typically seven to eight years, and selection from finest vineyard parcels define these bottlings, which are released in small quantities with vintage-specific stories.
Gusbourne's Fifty One Degrees North (2016, £195) and magnum (£395) exemplify the segment's ambition, while Langham's Perpetual Blanc de Blancs employs solera ageing inspired by grower Champagne.
Squerryes's Patience 2014, launched July 2026, connects the prestige cuvée to the Warde family's 300-year ownership and 17th-century wool merchant heritage linking England to Champagne trade.

MARKET.head: Centre-Loire rivals offer Sauvignon Blanc value as Sancerre prices soar above $40
MARKET.summ: Those interested in French wine are undoubtedly familiar with the Loire Valley, but digging a little deeper, there are many subregions within this expansive viticultural area to get to know. One of them is the Centre-Loire. And although the slightly misleading name suggests it’s the center of France’s lengthy and endlessly...
takeaways: Sancerre Sauvignon Blanc now sells for $40 to $50 per bottle, with production capped at current levels and no plans to expand vineyard area.

Five neighboring Centre-Loire appellations, Pouilly-Fumé, Menetou-Salon, Quincy, Reuilly, and Coteaux du Giennois, produce comparable Sauvignon Blancs and Pinot Noirs at $20 to $30, gaining market share from price-sensitive buyers.
Sancerre exports nearly three-quarters of its production, with half to the US, while exports from neighboring appellations remain smaller but growing.

Winemakers in the region now face climate-driven harvest acceleration, with 2024 potentially starting as early as August 20, forcing experimentation with abandoned acidic varieties to preserve freshness.
Pinot Noir from the region is improving in quality and emerging as an alternative to Burgundy at better value, according to producers including Matthieu Delaporte at Domaine Delaporte.

MARKET.head: Celebrity wine launches surge from 2005 peak to 2020 flood
MARKET.summ: The alcohol industry has seen an influx of celebrity-owned brands in recent decades, and the wine category is not immune to the trend. Whether birthed from genuine wine connoisseurship or just a marketing ploy, celebrity wine brands now make up a considerable sector of the industry. Famous people amass dedicated followers, and...
takeaways: Kyle MacLachlan launched Pursued by Bear in Walla Walla in 2005, marking an early entry by actors into wine ownership and production.
A wave of celebrity wine brands accelerated sharply in 2020, with Post Malone, Cameron Diaz, Snoop Dogg, and Mary J. Blige all launching lines that year during pandemic lockdowns.
Celebrity wine brands leverage existing fan bases to drive sales; Kylie Minogue's rosés became best-selling pink wines in the U.K. within years of launch.
The brands span multiple styles and price points, from organic-focused Avaline to fruit-forward blends, capturing different consumer segments and distribution channels.
Most celebrity labels partner with established winemakers and producers rather than operate independently, outsourcing production to focus on brand and marketing.

MARKET.head: Soju surges in U.S. market while shōchū lags, driven by Asian food and younger drinkers
MARKET.summ: As consumer interest grows, soju, shōchū, and baijiu are following distinct paths in the U.S. market, signaling that Asian spirits are evolving beyond a single trend
takeaways: Soju sales rose 133 percent between 2019 and 2025 in the U.S., now under one percent of total spirits volume, while shōchū grew only 11 percent over the same period, reflecting soju's acceleration post-2020.

Growth drivers include expansion of Asian cuisine restaurants, K-pop and K-drama cultural interest, younger consumers seeking lower-ABV and flavored spirits, and mass availability of affordable green-bottle brands like Jinro.

Spec's wine retailer in Texas increased Asian spirits purchases from under $1 million in 2018 to multi-millions today, with soju now a high-performer that forces the buyer to reject new brand pitches.

Craft soju makers like Tokki Soju in Brooklyn faced resistance from establishments favoring mass-produced green-bottle soju but achieved explosive growth by educating accounts on premium expressions pre-1965 Korean distilling styles.
Shōchū brands iichiko and Mizu target bartenders as key ambassadors, emphasizing higher-proof options around 40 percent ABV for cocktail applications to compete with tequila and mezcal drinkers.

MARKET.head: U.S. spirits exporters face tariff barriers as DISCUS seeks new markets
MARKET.summ: The hits just keep coming in the ongoing trade war, with President Trump announcing a new 50 percent tariff on Canadian whisky, beer, wine, and other products on July 20. That import tax, scheduled to start August 19, was described as a “necessary and appropriate” response to the removal of U.S. spirits from the shelves of most...
takeaways: The Distilled Spirits Council of the United States (DISCUS) is pursuing $900,000 in federal grants to boost U.S. spirits exports as tariffs block traditional markets in Canada, the EU, and Brazil.
Canada cut U.S. alcoholic beverage sales by 81 percent in retaliation for Trump administration tariffs; Brazil now faces a 25 percent U.S. tariff, complicating export plans.

India reduced its tariff on U.S. spirits from 150 percent to 100 percent last year, but new EU and U.K. trade deals offer Scotch and Irish whiskey rates of 40 percent and 75 percent, disadvantaging American competitors.

In India, a market of 1.4 billion people consuming the world's largest whiskey volume by quantity, bars like Four Seasons Bengaluru report strong demand for American bourbon among enthusiasts despite high tariffs.

Vietnam's emerging cocktail scene shows growing interest in American whiskey, though Scotch currently dominates; DISCUS is funding consumer education programs in key markets to build category awareness.

MARKET.head: 2026 World Cup drove US breweries to record on-premise sales and foot traffic
MARKET.summ: With soccer fans drinking taprooms dry and weekday draft beer sales up, the 2026 World Cup was a win for the beer industry. Can breweries leverage this playbook for future events?
takeaways: Breweries across North America reported volume surges during the June-July 2026 World Cup, with draft beer sales up 6.46 percent overall and 16 percent on Mondays and Tuesdays.
Headlands Brewing in California doubled production of its collaborative West Coast Mexican lager Common Ground from 90 to 180 barrels after initial stocks sold within weeks.

On-premise venues installed infrastructure and hosted watch parties; Boulevard Brewing's Kansas City taproom saw 25 percent foot traffic growth since mid-June, while Bitburger's on-premise sales rose 130 percent.
Newport Craft Brewing scaled It's Called Soccer from a planned 30 barrels to 300 barrels distributed across 315 venues in three states, now planning year-round distribution.

Breweries credited the World Cup with reviving casual drinking occasions lost during the pandemic, particularly among younger drinkers, and plan to leverage sports sponsorships for future sales growth.

MARKET.head: RNDC files Chapter 11 bankruptcy after shedding majority of US markets
MARKET.summ: Republic National Distributing Company (RNDC), formerly the second-largest wine and spirits distributor in the United States, has filed for bankruptcy after a yearlong shakedown. The distributor voluntarily filed for chapter 11 yesterday in the Southern District of Texas to initiate a court-facilitated process of shuttering the...
takeaways: Republic National Distributing Company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Texas federal court yesterday after a year of contraction, seeking court oversight to sell remaining operations and wind down.

RNDC lists liabilities between $1 billion and $10 billion against assets of $500 million to $1 billion, with over 100,000 creditors and $300 million in top unsecured claims led by Proximo Spirits' $93.92 million trade debt.

The distributor shed California operations last June, then sold 11 markets to Reyes Beverage Group and stakes to Columbia Distributing, Martignetti Companies, and BreakThru Beverage Group while claiming to preserve 5,000 jobs.
Roughly 1,450 workers remain employed; RNDC sought immediate court permission to continue payroll and benefits to prevent staff exodus during reorganization.
Small suppliers holding unsecured claims face high risk of total loss, as they lack leverage to demand prepayment and cannot easily route products through competing distributors.

CULTURE.head: Decanter World Wine Awards 2026 sees record medal counts across regions
CULTURE.summ: Despite (or perhaps because of ) the headwinds buffeting the wine industry, this year’s Decanter World Wine Awards (DWWA) saw a dramatic uptick in quality. Our DWWA Co-Chair and Decanter Contributing Editor runs his analytical eye over this year’s results, highlights and revelations
takeaways: Decanter World Wine Awards 2026 received 16,631 entries judged by 245 experts including 106 women, a record female judge count.
Platinum medals rose to 196 (1.2% of entries), Gold to 924 (5.6%), and Silver to 6,193 (37.2%), each category increasing significantly versus 2025.
Cool-climate regions gained ground: Oxfordshire won its first Gold; New Zealand took two Best in Show and eight Platinums; Savoie took Platinum and two Value Golds.
Warm-climate producers excelled with 52.4% more top medals than 2025: Spain achieved Platinum for Jumilla, Castilla-La Mancha and Priorat; Rías Baixas took Best in Show.
Germany's top medal went to Weisser Burgunder from Pfalz rather than Riesling, reflecting judges' recognition of shifting ripeness and styles across regions.

CULTURE.head: Ancient vine-training systems decline as labor costs and mechanization pressure historic landscapes
CULTURE.summ: As labor costs soar, global wine regions are forced to weigh the high expense of traditional vineyard design against its tourism appeal and climate-adapting benefits
takeaways: Italy's alberata system, shown in 1793 paintings intertwining vines with trees across Naples, survives on only a handful of hectares today, replaced by mechanizable methods like Guyot.

Lanzarote's hoyo pits, carved after 1730-1736 volcanic eruptions to reach soil beneath lapilli ash, drew thousands of tourists and supported the island's economy until labor demands forced 19 percent vineyard abandonment between 2000 and 2026.
Alberto González Plasencia of Bodegas Timanfaya and Juan Glaria of Bodegas Rubicon warn that without subsidies, Lanzarote's hoyos will disappear and tourist visits, and wine values, will follow.

Familia Torres maintains Rías Baixas pergola training for Albariño on six hectares at Pazo Torre Panelas using specialized machinery, viable because the region's DO bans mechanized harvesting across all systems.

Veneto's 19th-century bellussera pergola-alberata hybrid, which once supported silk production and livestock, covers nine percent of Piave DOC but may survive through climate-change adaptation and wine tourism, if regions balance heritage with economics.

CULTURE.head: Brooklyn housing complex installs pathways from 450,000 recycled wine corks
CULTURE.summ: Wine bottle corks are getting a second lease on life in New York City. Earlier this month, a New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) project in Brooklyn cut the ribbon on newly paved pathways and playground surfaces made of upcycled corks. The first-of-its-kind installation is part of the nonprofit Public Housing Community...
takeaways: Corks were ground and mixed with adhesive at a Wisconsin recycling center, then laid as playing surfaces that absorb stormwater, reduce ambient temperature by 20 to 30 percent, and replace toxic plastic or rubber.

Resident children at Marlboro Houses submitted design mockups reviewed by Center for Justice Innovation, The Urban Conga design studio, and the Marlboro Resident Association, who shaped the final layout.
Global cork production reaches 13 billion stoppers annually, yet less than one percent are recycled; three billion are discarded in the US each year.

SCIENCE.head: Disease-resistant hybrids cut fungicide sprays 80%, gain European vineyard ground
SCIENCE.summ: Fungus-resistant hybrid grape varieties, known as PIWIs, are evolving through advances in breeding, offering growers new options in a changing climate
takeaways: PIWIs (fungus-resistant hybrid grapes) reduce fungicide sprays from 8-15 times yearly to 2-3, cutting chemical, fuel, and labor costs by up to 80 percent.
German breeders pioneered modern PIWIs in the late 20th century; today's varieties contain up to 95 percent Vitis vinifera genetic material while retaining mildew resistance from American species.

Genetic technology rhAmpSeq, adopted globally since 2019, identifies disease-resistance genes with precision and cuts breeding timescales from months to days via marker-assisted selection of seedlings.

Germany leads adoption with 4,000 hectares of PIWI plantings in 2025 (4 percent of vineyard area, 10 percent annual growth); France develops ResDur hybrids bred to maintain regional signature varieties like Cabernet Franc.
Luxembourg 2026 study showed PIWIs delivered twofold economic savings and threefold environmental gains; retail expansion accelerating as supermarket chains stock PIWIs alongside traditional wines.

SCIENCE.head: Vineyards use netting to cool fruit zones as heat stress intensifies
SCIENCE.summ: Netting is no longer just for hail, it is becoming one of viticulture's most versatile climate adaptation tools
takeaways: Vineyard netting, traditionally used for hail and bird protection, is now deployed to lower cluster temperatures and preserve color, acidity, and phenolics during heat events.
UC Davis research on Cabernet Sauvignon found shaded clusters had 27 percent more anthocyanins than unshaded fruit when temperatures exceeded 35 degrees Celsius during heat spikes.

At Petra in Tuscany, Marco Simonit's 2025 trials showed Merlot clusters under nets measured 40–41 degrees Celsius versus 50 degrees in unshaded controls, reducing sunburn from 41 percent to three percent.
Luis Reginato at Catena Zapata in Mendoza found nets intercept just 15 percent of radiation in high-altitude vineyards, allowing filtered light while reducing water stress on vines.
Net color and placement matter critically: white or green nets perform better than black, and nets must stay away from clusters to avoid heat damage from contact with the material itself.

SCIENCE.head: Grape sunburn spreads north as heat waves force vineyard practice shifts
SCIENCE.summ: As climate change makes heat waves more prevalent, more producers have to combat sunburn in grapes, and the flabby, flat, rubbery notes they can bring to wine
takeaways: Sunburn in grapes is a stress response to excess light and heat that degrades chlorophyll, polyphenols, and aromatic compounds, producing flavors of asphalt, rubber, and leather in the finished wine.
Berry surface temperatures can reach 122°F on a 95°F day; Chardonnay shows damage within five minutes at 104-109°F under high light, while cell death occurs at 126°F.
Producers in warm regions including Provence and Napa now avoid mid-summer leaf removal, limit defoliation to east-facing sides only, and skip it entirely for white varieties due to heat-wave risk.
Tyrrell's in Australia's Hunter Valley has used kaolin clay spray since 2014 to cool canopy by up to nine degrees Celsius, while Matthiasson Wines redesigns trellis and orientation to shade fruit.
Climate change is pushing sunburn damage into regions that never faced it before, forcing growers to prioritize canopy cover and sorting over traditional sun-exposure practices.

NEWSLETTERS.head: The new releases from Radford Dale, including Elgin and Vinum bottlings from 2025
NEWSLETTERS.summ: I have been following the wines of Radford Dale with some interest over the last three years. The
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Petroné Thomas was promoted to winemaker at Radford Dale in 2024 and took responsibility for Elgin wines after Jacques de Klerk departed later that year.
Radford Dale Elgin Estate will plant Cabernet Franc to replace Semillon vineyards; currently only 0.4ha of Cabernet Franc exists in the ground.
The 2025 vintage marks the final Semillon release from Radford Dale Elgin Estate as vineyards are being regrafted to Cabernet Franc.
First crop of young Chardonnay and Pinot Noir vines (planted 2022) harvested in 2026; Gamay 'Antidote' name returning with 900 litres from new plantings.
No 2024 Frankenstein or Renaissance bottlings released; 2024 fruit redirected to Vinum bottlings due to lack of desired directness in the wines.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Michelin And The Death Of The Wine Guide
NEWSLETTERS.summ: It was entirely predictable that Michelin’s new venture into wine would trigger huffy French recriminations. Its Wine Selection Burgundy 2026, launched this month, awarded nine producers the top accolade of three grapes, another 20 vignerons two grapes, and 33 one grape. A further 32 were merely “selected”.
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Michelin's Wine Selection Burgundy 2026 awarded nine producers three grapes, 20 two grapes, 33 one grape, and 32 "selected" status.
Domaine Arnoux-Lachaux publicly demanded removal from Michelin's guide after receiving only one grape despite being a celebrated Vosne-Romanée house.
Michelin rates producers based on vineyard management and consistency rather than individual wines, unlike competitor Guide Hachette des Vins which rates cuvées one to five.

Consumer wine guides emerged in the 1970s with Decanter, Wine Spectator, Hugh Johnson's Pocket Wine Book (1977), and Parker's Wine Advocate, but internet availability and vast wine expansion have eroded their utility.
Michelin's wine venture signals the end of traditional consumer wine guides, with future advice increasingly driven by AI apps rather than human-authored publications.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Six Wines That Stopped Me in My Tracks
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Exceptional new discoveries from Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Charly, originally from Burgundy, moved to Lower Austria a decade ago and produces wines under his own label with a French sensibility.
Charly's Blauer Portugieser, sourced from grapes grown by Christoph Hoch, offers ripeness and creamy texture atypical of the variety.
Charly's Grüner Veltliner 2022, Blaufränkisch 2023, and Zweigelt 2023 are available from Gute Weine for €27 per bottle with EU delivery.
Charly sources grapes from friends farming organically or biodynamically for his wines while owning just one hectare of vines.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Notable Releases from Troon Vineyard
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Notes on a Vermentino and two Syrahs, one with some bottle age
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Troon Vineyard released 2025 Vermentino and 2023 Syrah from Oregon's Applegate Valley.
Troon Vineyard practices certified biodynamic and regenerative organic farming in Grant's Pass.
Troon uses ambient cultures for fermentation, minimal sulfites, and neutral or alternative vessels, no new oak.
Applegate Valley's alluvial soils, Mediterranean heat, and cold overnight temperatures from Siskiyou Mountains suit sun-loving grapes.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A wine of straw
NEWSLETTERS.summ: "Why all the grape drying?" "For something beautiful my boy!"
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: Dessert wine consumption has declined for approximately 75 years and shows no signs of recovery.
Raül Bobet, co-owner of Ferrer-Bobet in Priorat, Catalunya, released a dessert wine requiring 20 years of aging.
Goût Russe Champagne of the 19th century contained 300g/l of sugar, made for the Russian market.
